One moment shows the crack. Teiresias mentions 'the parents who begat thee,' and Oedipus, mid-fury, stops: 'Who begat me, speak?' It is the question under all his other questions, and it surfaces for a second before the anger closes over it. Then the seer gives his parting speech in the third person, about 'this man' who is brother and father to his own children. Either Oedipus has already turned away or he cannot take it in. The Chorus heard every word, and [[s4]] shows what they make of it.

annotations.quote: Mind you, I speak as one who comes a stranger
annotations.note: He means he arrived in Thebes after the murder. He is the one person present who was at the scene, and the one person present who was born in the palace behind him.

annotations.quote: The curse I laid on others fall on me.
annotations.note: A conscientious clause, added so that no one can say the king exempted his own house. It is the sentence he will insist on in [[s13]], 'by my own proclamation.'

annotations.quote: As though he were my sire, and leave no stone
annotations.note: The baldest irony in the play. 'As though' is the only inaccurate phrase in the line.

annotations.quote: Alas, alas, what misery to be wise
annotations.note: Teiresias enters already defeated by what he knows. Knowledge in this play is never a gift; ask Jocasta in [[s7]].

annotations.quote: Speak not to these or me. Thou art the man,
annotations.note: The seer simply applies the decree: the killer may speak to no one, so Oedipus must be silent. Storr's 'Thou art the man' borrows Nathan's words to King David, another ruler who condemned a criminal without knowing it was himself.

annotations.quote: In ear, wit, eye, in everything art blind.
annotations.note: The taunt comes back on him word for word. When he has put out his eyes he will wish he could stop his ears as well.

annotations.quote: The simple Oedipus; _I_ stopped her mouth
annotations.note: The italic is Storr's, catching an emphatic Greek pronoun. 'Simple' is mock-modest: the know-nothing outsider who did what the professionals could not. The Greek ear may also catch 'oida,' I know, inside his name.

annotations.quote: This day shall be thy birth-day, and thy grave.
annotations.note: Today he will learn who bore him, and that knowledge will end the life he has lived. A riddle, handed to the riddle-solver, and he cannot read it.

annotations.quote: He passes for an alien in the land
annotations.note: The prophecy reverses every term of the proclamation: the 'stranger' is a native, the avenger is the killer, the king will leave as a blind beggar feeling his way with a stick.

links.why: The conspiracy theory born here is tried out on Creon, and then collapses for an unexpected reason.
Every taunt about eyes and blindness is paid in full.
Oedipus enforces this scene's curse on himself.

s4.essay:
The Chorus have just heard their king called a murderer by the most trusted prophet in Thebes, and this song is them not knowing what to do with that. The first half looks away from the problem. They imagine the killer as someone else entirely, a fugitive out in the wild, 'like a sullen bull' in the upland woods, with Apollo and the Fates behind him 'like sleuth-hounds.' It is a vivid picture and wrong in every detail: the hunted man is not fleeing through forests, he is inside the palace directing the hunt. Only one phrase lands, and by accident. 'A foot for flight he needs.' The name Oedipus means swollen-foot, and the play comes back to those feet in [[s7]].

The second half turns to face what Teiresias said, and I find it an honest piece of reasoning from decent men. They are 'sore perplexed.' They know of no quarrel between the house of Labdacus and 'Polybus' son,' which is what they and Oedipus both believe him to be. Gods know everything; but is a human prophet really wiser than any other man? Where is the proof? Against an unproven word they set a proven deed: he saved them from the Sphinx, 'like gold assayed.' So they side with the king. Loyalty, evidence and gratitude all point the same way, and all are mistaken. Keep this ode in mind at [[s6]], where the same singers find their trust much harder to hold.

annotations.quote: A foot for flight he needs
annotations.note: The killer must run fast. The man they are describing was pinned through the ankles as a baby and is named for it.

annotations.quote: Now like a sullen bull he roves
annotations.note: An outcast animal driven from the herd. The image is wrong today and right tomorrow: wandering the wilds, cut off from men, is what Oedipus will beg for in [[s13]].

annotations.quote: Twixt the Labdacidan house and our ruler, Polybus’ son.
annotations.note: The Labdacids are Laius' family, named for his father Labdacus. The elders can find no motive because they have the wrong father: they set against each other two houses that are one.

annotations.quote: Tested and tried in the light of us all, like gold assayed?
annotations.note: To assay gold is to test its purity. Their evidence is good as far as it goes. What it proves is cleverness and courage, which were never in doubt.

links.why: The accusation this ode is trying to absorb.
The next ode, where the same loyalty is under strain.

s5.essay:
This is the longest stretch of the play and, to my mind, the best constructed. It begins as a political quarrel and ends with a man waiting for a witness who can destroy him, and the pivot between the two is a single phrase spoken by someone trying to help.

The Creon scene first. Oedipus comes out with his theory fully formed: 'My murderer and the filcher of my crown.' Creon's defence is cool, lawyerly, and not very lovable. Why would he want to be king when he already has a king's influence without a king's worries? 'I am not so infatuate as to grasp / The shadow when I hold the substance fast.' It is the reasoning of a comfortable man, and it happens to be true. Oedipus is not listening. Asked whether he wants Creon banished, he says no: dead. This is the worst we see of him, and Sophocles lets it be bad. Creon's exit line is worth keeping: 'Such tempers justly plague themselves the most.' In a play about a plague, the verb is not casual.

It takes Jocasta and the Chorus together, in a short sung exchange, to make Oedipus relent, and he does it gracelessly. Then the Chorus try to drop the subject ('better sleeping ills to leave at rest') and Jocasta will not let them. It is the first of several moments where the inquiry could stop and does not.

Now the hinge. Jocasta wants to calm her husband, and her method is to prove that prophets know nothing. Her evidence: an oracle once told Laius he would die by his own son's hand, and look, the child was put out on a mountain at three days old with its ankles pinned, and Laius was killed by strangers 'at a spot where three roads meet.' Every element of the speech is meant as comfort. And one incidental detail, mentioned only for colour, goes into Oedipus like a blade. 'What memories, what wild tumult of the soul.' He does not react to the pinned ankles, though he has carried the scars all his life. He reacts to the crossroads. I think that is psychologically right: he is thinking as a man accused of murder, and he hears the evidence that bears on the murder.

The questions that follow are the kind he put to Creon in [[s1]], but the temperature has changed. Where? When? What did Laius look like? Jocasta's answer is one of the quietest terrible lines in the play: tall, going grey, 'and not unlike thee in form.' She is describing a father to his son and neither can hear it.

Then Oedipus tells his own story for the first time, and we get the life from the inside: the drunk at the banquet in Corinth, the taunt that 'rankled,' the secret trip to Delphi, the oracle that answered a different question from the one he asked. He fled Corinth to protect Polybus and Merope. That is the fact I would most want a first-time reader to hold on to. Everything Oedipus did to escape the prophecy was decent, and every step of it was a step toward Thebes. The killing itself he tells without much remorse: an old man in a carriage struck him, he struck back, 'and so I slew them every one.' The temper we watched in [[s3]] was there at the crossroads too.

Notice exactly how much he now fears. He fears he killed Laius, and that his own curse has fallen on him: banishment from Thebes, with no return to Corinth, lest he harm the parents he still believes are his. The larger truth is not in view at all. He thinks he may be a regicide. He does not dream he is a son.

So the scene ends on arithmetic. The survivor said robbers, plural, and 'one' and 'many' cannot square. If the herdsman keeps to his story, Oedipus is clear. It is a real point, and the play never resolves it; by the time the man arrives in [[s9]] nobody remembers to ask. Jocasta, meanwhile, closes with a flourish: whatever the herdsman says, the oracle about her child failed, for the 'poor babe' died first. 'So much for divination.' She has just disproved prophecy with the story of its fulfilment.

annotations.quote: I know not; to my sovereign’s acts I am blind.
annotations.note: A courtier's tact, in the play's most loaded word. Everyone in Thebes is blind in some degree; the Chorus's version is choosing not to look.

annotations.quote: Thy Thebans? am not I a Theban too?
annotations.note: Creon's best retort, sharper than he knows. He is speaking to a born Theban who thinks himself a naturalized foreigner.

annotations.quote: No natives, at a spot where three roads meet.
annotations.note: The sentence on which the play turns, and Jocasta throws it away as a detail. 'No natives' is the comforting part and the false part.

annotations.quote: When Laius, its ankles pierced and pinned
annotations.note: She says Laius did it. The herdsman will say in [[s9]] that she handed him the child herself. Whether she is sparing herself or Storr is compressing, it is the first hint of what this calm woman has lived with.

annotations.quote: With silver; and not unlike thee in form.
annotations.note: Asked to describe her first husband, she finds the nearest comparison standing in front of her.

annotations.quote: That in the end the seer will prove not blind.
annotations.note: Only a scene ago he was mocking Teiresias' eyes. The metaphor has already begun to turn round in his own mouth.

annotations.quote: A roisterer at some banquet, flown with wine,
annotations.note: 'Flown' is flushed, swollen with drink; Storr has it from Milton. The whole catastrophe is set moving by a drunk at a dinner party, the only person in Corinth who told Oedipus the truth.

annotations.quote: Still speaks of robbers, not a robber, I
annotations.note: The detective's mind is still working under the fear: a single testable fact, one witness to settle it. He is right about the method and it will not save him.

annotations.quote: So much for divination. Henceforth I
annotations.note: Jocasta is no villain for this. She gave up a child to an oracle and, as she believes, got nothing for it. Her scepticism is grief that has hardened. The Chorus are shocked all the same, as [[s6]] shows.

links.why: The curse Oedipus now fears he laid on himself, and the seer he begins to believe.
Jocasta's proof against oracles gets what looks like a second confirmation, and then comes apart.
The witness sent for here arrives, and is asked a different question.

s6.essay:
This is the hardest ode in the play and the one I would least want skipped. The elders have just heard their queen say 'So much for divination,' and their king agree that she reasons well. They answer with a hymn to the laws 'ordained on high,' which no mortal made and which do not grow old, and then with a stanza on the tyrant, bred of 'insolence' (the Greek word is hybris), who climbs to the top and 'topples o'er.'

Whom do they mean? Not simply Oedipus, I think; they still pray heaven to keep 'the true patriot.' But they have watched him threaten a blind priest and sentence his brother-in-law to death without trial in [[s5]], and the song is uneasy in a way [[s4]] was not. The loyalty is still there. The certainty is gone.

The last stanzas are startling. If oracles turn out false, they say, they will stop going to Delphi: 'Why dance I still and lead the sacred choir?' That line steps half outside the play. A chorus, dancing in a theatre at a festival of a god, asks what the point of dancing would be. They want the prophecy about Laius to come true, because the alternative is a world with nothing behind it. Think what that means. These loyal men are praying, without quite seeing it, for the destruction of their king. 'Apollo is forsook and faith grows cold,' they end, and at that moment Jocasta walks out carrying incense for Apollo.

annotations.quote: The tyrant; insolence full blown,
annotations.note: 'Insolence' translates hybris: not rudeness but the overreaching of a man who forgets he is mortal. 'Tyrant' in Greek meant a ruler who took power rather than inheriting it, which is what everyone believes Oedipus to be. He is in fact the legitimate heir.

annotations.quote: Why dance I still and lead the sacred choir?
annotations.note: The most self-aware line the Chorus have. If the gods' word fails, worship is a pantomime, and so is the play we are watching.

annotations.quote: His weird, men heed it not;
annotations.note: 'Weird' is the old noun for fate or destiny, as in Macbeth's weird sisters. Here it means the oracle given to Laius, which Jocasta has just laughed off.

annotations.quote: Apollo is forsook and faith grows cold.
annotations.note: The entrance that follows is timed against this line: the sceptic comes out to pray. Sophocles is not mocking her. Fear has done what argument could not.

links.why: The dismissal of oracles that provokes this ode.
The earlier, easier loyalty, for contrast.
Jocasta's prayer to the god she has just dismissed, and its instant answer.

s7.essay:
The scene opens with a small, bitter joke. Jocasta, who has just announced she will never again look for signs, comes out with wreaths to pray to Apollo, since her own counsels 'naught avail.' And the prayer is answered at once: a messenger walks in with what looks like deliverance. Sophocles times it so that the god seems to reply. He does, though not as asked.

The Corinthian is one of my favourite minor figures in Greek drama. He is cheerful, a little self-interested (he admits he came hoping 'to profit'), and eager to please. His news is that Polybus is dead of old age, and for a few lines the stage is almost giddy. Jocasta crows over the oracles; Oedipus joins her: 'Dust, ashes, nothing, dead as Polybus.' It is the high point of their confidence, and Jocasta draws the philosophy from it: man is 'the sport of chance,' so 'best live a careless life.' Her remark that many a man has slept with his mother in dreams is offered as a shrug. Freud built a theory on that line. In context it is a woman telling her husband not to worry.

But Oedipus is thorough. Half the oracle remains, and Merope is alive. So the messenger, wanting only to remove a last anxiety, removes the floor: Polybus 'was naught to thee in blood.' The pattern of [[s5]] repeats exactly. Jocasta tried to comfort him and gave him the crossroads; this man tries to comfort him and gives him Cithaeron, the pinned feet, the name itself. Good intentions are the engine of this plot.

Watch Jocasta during the questioning. She says nothing for some fifty lines, and somewhere in that silence she understands everything: the ankles, the mountain, the shepherd of Laius' house. When she speaks again it is only to beg him to stop. Oedipus, wonderfully and horribly, misreads her. He thinks she is a snob, afraid her husband will prove slave-born. Her last words to him refuse every name she might use, husband or son, and settle on 'poor wretch.' Then silence 'evermore.' She goes in to die, and we learn how in [[s11]].

What Oedipus says next is the speech I find most moving in the play, because it is so wrong and so alive. He calls himself Fortune's child, with the months for brothers. 'Nothing can make me other than I am.' He means it as defiance. It is the plainest statement of his doom.

annotations.quote: To thee, our present help in time of trouble,
annotations.note: Storr gives the pagan queen the language of Psalm 46. She turns to Apollo because, in the Greek, his altar is simply the nearest one. It is piety as a last resort.

annotations.quote: This is his queen the mother of his children.
annotations.note: In the Greek the word order lets an audience hear 'this is his wife and mother' for a beat before 'of his children' arrives. Storr's unpunctuated line keeps a little of that stumble.

annotations.quote: My son, ’tis plain, thou know’st not what thou doest.
annotations.note: An old man's familiar 'my son,' which is nearer the truth than he intends: he carried this king as a baby. Storr's wording also echoes the Gospel's 'they know not what they do,' fairly enough.

annotations.quote: Dust, ashes, nothing, dead as Polybus.
annotations.note: Oedipus at his most reckless, celebrating a father's death because it clears him. Even here he pauses to wonder whether Polybus died of missing him. He cannot stop testing the oracle for loopholes.

annotations.quote: Best live a careless life from hand to mouth.
annotations.note: 'Careless' in the old sense: free of care. Jocasta's creed is that nothing is foreseen, so nothing need be feared. She will hold it for perhaps five more minutes.

annotations.quote: Whence thou deriv’st the name that still is thine.
annotations.note: Oedipus means 'swollen-foot.' He has answered to a description of his own wound all his life without asking where it came from. The evidence was in his name and his body the whole time.

annotations.quote: Ah mayst thou ne’er discover who thou art!
annotations.note: The only prayer left to her, and the opposite of the Delphic command to know thyself. She knows already; this line is love trying to keep him ignorant.

annotations.quote: Who rank myself as Fortune’s favorite child,
annotations.note: He would rather be the son of pure Chance than of anyone in particular. Jocasta said a moment ago that chance rules everything. He has taken her philosophy just as she has lost it.

links.why: The first time a comforting speech handed Oedipus a clue; the ankles were mentioned there too.
The other shepherd arrives and the two halves of the story meet.
What Jocasta does after 'silent evermore.'

s8.essay:
A short, bright, mistaken song. Oedipus has just declared himself the child of Fortune and stands waiting for the herdsman, and the Chorus catch his mood and run with it. If the king was found on Cithaeron, then Cithaeron shall be honoured as his 'nurse and foster-mother,' and by tomorrow's full moon there will be dancing. And who were his parents? Perhaps a nymph. Perhaps Pan was the father, or Apollo, or Hermes ('Cyllene's lord'), or Bacchus. A foundling on a mountain, in the old stories, is usually a god's bastard.

Sophocles likes to do this: put a burst of joy immediately before the blow. It makes the fall steeper, and here it also tells us something about the elders. A few minutes ago, in [[s6]], they were afraid that the oracles were failing. Now they call their own soul 'prophetic' and prophesy nonsense. They are not stupid. They love this man and want his mystery to be a glorious one.

The cruelty is in the particulars. Cithaeron will be named again, by Oedipus himself in [[s13]], as the place that should have killed him. And the father they guess at with such pleasure is a question with a mortal answer. The one god they name who truly had a hand in it is Loxias, and not as a lover of nymphs.

annotations.quote: Thee, Cithaeron, I shall hail,
annotations.note: The mountain between Thebes and Corinth, where the baby was left. Teiresias named it in [[s3]] as the place that would echo with Oedipus' cries. The Chorus have forgotten.

annotations.quote: Ere tomorrow’s full moon rises, and exalt thee as is meet.
annotations.note: A deadline, and an accurate one: by tomorrow everything about his birth will indeed be known. 'As is meet' means as is fitting.

annotations.quote: did Loxias beget thee, for he haunts the upland wold;
annotations.note: Loxias is Apollo in his role as giver of oracles; a 'wold' is open hill country. They imagine the god as Oedipus' father. He is nearer to being his author.

links.why: The anxious ode this one forgets.
The real answer to 'who bare thee' follows at once.

s9.essay:
Everything in the play has been narrowing toward this meeting, and when it comes it is tiny: three men, a few minutes, most of it in single lines. I think it the most perfectly made scene in ancient drama, and part of the perfection is economy. Sophocles has made one old man do two jobs. The herdsman now shuffling in is the sole survivor of the crossroads, sent for in [[s5]] to say whether one man or many killed Laius. He is also the servant who was given a baby to expose. Oedipus summoned a witness to a murder; he gets a witness to a birth, and the question about numbers is never asked. It no longer needs asking.

The two shepherds are beautifully contrasted. The Corinthian is all bonhomie: remember those three summers on Cithaeron, you with two flocks, me with one? He thinks he is arranging a happy reunion. The Theban's reply is a curse. He has known since he came back from the crossroads and found the killer on the throne; that, we now understand, is why he begged Jocasta to send him to the far pastures. He has kept this silence for most of his life.

And Oedipus tortures him. I do not want to soften that. 'Arrest the villain, seize and pinion him!' An old man's arms are twisted behind him by a king threatening death, and what is wrung out of him is the king's own ruin. Yet this is also where Oedipus is greatest. The herdsman says he stands on 'the perilous edge of speech,' and Oedipus answers that he stands on the edge of hearing, 'but I still must hear.' He knows by then. He could stop, as Jocasta begged him to in [[s7]]. He will not buy safety with ignorance, and that refusal is his dignity as surely as his temper is his fault.

The last facts come in half-lines, as if neither man can bear a whole one. Jocasta gave the child. To destroy it. Because of the oracle. Why then did you give it away? 'Through pity, master, for the babe.' That is the answer that undoes me. Not malice, not even fate in any grand sense: a slave could not bring himself to kill a baby. Pity saved Oedipus for this.

His cry is to the light, which he asks never to see again. Teiresias promised as much in [[s3]].

annotations.quote: A simple hind, but true as any man.
annotations.note: A 'hind' is a farm servant. The Chorus vouch for his honesty before he speaks, and he is honest: that is why he has hidden on the hills for so long rather than lie to his king's face.

annotations.quote: Friend, he that stands before thee was that child.
annotations.note: Said with a flourish, by a man expecting a reward. The Corinthian never understands what he has done. He is the most innocent person in the play and its most efficient destroyer.

annotations.quote: A plague upon thee! Hold thy wanton tongue!
annotations.note: Storr's idiom is apter than the herdsman could know. The plague is the reason any of them are standing here.

annotations.quote: And I of hearing, but I still must hear.
annotations.note: For me the best line Oedipus has. All day others have tried to stop him: Teiresias, the Chorus, Jocasta, now this slave. The same stubbornness that damned Creon unheard here becomes courage.

annotations.quote: Through pity, master, for the babe. I thought
annotations.note: The moral centre of the story, given to a nameless slave. Two kindnesses, his and the Corinthian's, did what Laius' cruelty tried to prevent. Oedipus curses that pity in [[s12]].

annotations.quote: O light, may I behold thee nevermore!
annotations.note: He says it before he does it. The blinding in [[s11]] is not a frenzy that comes from nowhere; it is this sentence carried out.

links.why: Why this man was sent for, and the question about 'one' and 'many' that is never put to him.
The Corinthian's half of the story, and Jocasta's plea to stop.
What 'O light, may I behold thee nevermore' leads to.

s10.essay:
With Oedipus gone inside, the Chorus sing the thought the whole play has been building toward, and they do not make it small. They do not say he was wicked, or proud. They say he was the best of us, and look. 'Races of mortal man,' they begin, 'I count ye but the shadow of a shade.' Oedipus becomes the example for everyone. If the man who 'outshot the rest' and beat the Sphinx had only the 'show' of happiness, then no one can be called blest.

I notice how carefully they keep their gratitude. The second stanza is a full account of what he did for them, and the ode ends by holding both truths at once: 'through thee I drew new breath, / And now through thee I feel a second death.' This is the same chorus that could not believe Teiresias in [[s4]], and their loyalty has not turned to disgust. It has turned to mourning; they sing 'a dirge as o'er the dead' for a man still alive.

The third stanza is where they name the thing itself, with an agricultural metaphor that comes from the Greek: the wife as a field the father ploughed. The same image returns, harsher, in [[s11]]. And then 'All-seeing Time hath caught' him. The detective, in the end, was Time, and the inquiry that Oedipus opened in [[s1]] is closed.

annotations.quote: I count ye but the shadow of a shade!
annotations.note: Storr's phrase for a Greek line that says, roughly, 'I count you as equal to nothing.' Note the plural: one man's fall is taken at once as a measure of all human happiness.

annotations.quote: Thy cradle was thy marriage bed;
annotations.note: Seven words for the whole horror. The Greek speaks of one harbour serving both son and father, and Storr keeps that in the next line.

annotations.quote: How could the soil thy father eared so long
annotations.note: To 'ear' is an old word for to plough. The image treats Jocasta as land, which is hard to like, but it makes the incest a violation of natural order, the same order whose crops are now blighted.

annotations.quote: And now through thee I feel a second death.
annotations.note: He gave the city its life back from the Sphinx, and now takes it down with him. The Priest feared exactly this epitaph in [[s1]].

links.why: The Priest's 'first of men' and his fear of a king who raised the city only to cast it down.
The Chorus's last word draws the same moral.

s11.essay:
Greek tragedy keeps its violence offstage and has it told, and a first-time reader may feel cheated: the two most shocking events in the story happen behind a door. I would argue the opposite. The Second Messenger's speech is the most frightening thing in the play precisely because it is a report, by a shaken servant, of what he could and could not see.

Notice what he could not. Jocasta runs to the bedroom and shuts the doors 'with a crash,' and from then on she is only a voice, calling on Laius, cursing the bed where she bore 'husband by husband, children by her child.' The servants never see her die, because Oedipus bursts in and 'all eyes were fixed' on him. Even in her death she is upstaged. It is a small, exact cruelty, and it fits how the play has treated her: she understood first, in [[s7]], and left without a scene.

Oedipus comes in asking for a sword. For whom? The messenger does not say, and I think we are meant to fear he would have used it on her. Instead he finds her hanging, takes her down, and uses what is at hand: the gold pins from her dress. That detail matters to me more than any other. He blinds himself with something of hers, beside the bed, over her body. It is punishment and also, horribly, a last act of their marriage.

His stated reason is strange and worth reading slowly. The eyes are punished for what they failed to recognize: they saw those they 'should ne'er have seen' and did not know those he 'yearned to know.' It is a judgment on a kind of seeing. All through [[s3]] sight was his boast against Teiresias; now he makes the old man's prophecy literal with his own hands.

Then there is the messenger's opening verdict, that these are ills 'wrought of malice, not unwittingly.' Storr's 'malice' is odd; the sense is willed, not unwilled. The killing and the marriage were done in ignorance. The blinding is the first thing in the story that Oedipus does knowing exactly what he is doing. 'The worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds.' I am not sure that is true, but it marks the line the rest of the play walks, between what was done to him and what he did.

And then the doors open. He wants to be seen.

annotations.quote: The worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds.
annotations.note: The messenger means the suicide and the blinding. It reaches further: the curse, the inquiry and the insistence on hearing were all self-inflicted too.

annotations.quote: Nor could we mark her agony to the end.
annotations.note: Jocasta's death goes unwitnessed even by the witness. Sophocles gives us a closed door and a cry of 'Laius,' and lets the imagination do the rest.

annotations.quote: No mortal, surely, none of us who watched him
annotations.note: No servant told him where she was; something 'supernal' steered him. The messenger offers the divine explanation here. Oedipus divides the responsibility more exactly in [[s12]].

annotations.quote: He tore the golden brooches that upheld
annotations.note: Long pins that fastened a woman's robe at the shoulders. Pinned ankles at the start of his life, pins in the eyes at the end of his reign: I doubt the symmetry is accidental.

annotations.quote: Those ye should ne’er have seen; now blind to those
annotations.note: He speaks to his own eyes as if to accomplices. In darkness they may look on the forbidden faces: perhaps the dead parents, perhaps the children. The riddle-solver's last utterance in the palace is itself a riddle.

annotations.quote: That shameful word my lips may not repeat.
annotations.note: The servant will quote 'slayer of his sire' but stops at the word for what Oedipus was to his mother. Parricide can be said aloud; this cannot.

links.why: Teiresias foretold the blindness, the beggar's staff and the exile.
'O light, may I behold thee nevermore' was said before it was done.
The man himself comes out and says whose hand it was.

s12.essay:
The doors open and the Chorus cannot look. 'Horror-struck away I turn,' they sing, in the same breath as admitting they long to stare and to ask questions. It is the honest response of anyone at an accident, and it is also ours: we came to the theatre to see exactly this.

What follows is sung, a lament shared between actor and chorus (a kommos), and the change from speech to song is the play's way of saying that argument has stopped. Oedipus' first words are not about guilt. They are about disorientation: where is he being carried, why does his own voice seem to float away from him? Blindness is new to him. Then he recognizes the Chorus by voice and thanks them for staying. I find that the most human moment in the play. The man who an hour ago could not hear what anyone was telling him now knows a friend by sound alone.

The Chorus ask what everyone asks: what power drove him to it? His answer is the most careful sentence he speaks. Apollo 'brought these ills to pass; / But the right hand that dealt the blow / Was mine, none other.' Both halves are meant. The god made the pattern; the man struck his own eyes. He will not hide behind fate, and he will not pretend fate was absent. People have argued for centuries about whether Oedipus is free or doomed, and here he simply declines the choice.

After that he curses the shepherd who unpinned his feet, the pity we saw in [[s9]], and the Chorus agree. They go further: better dead than blind. He does not accept that, and his reply opens [[s13]].

annotations.quote: My voice flits from me on the air!
annotations.note: A wonderfully exact observation of sudden blindness: without sight he cannot place even his own voice. The king who strode out in [[s1]] now has to ask where he is.

annotations.quote: I know thee near, and though bereft of eyes,
annotations.note: Recognition by ear. It is how Teiresias has always known the world, and Oedipus is learning it within minutes.

annotations.quote: Apollo, friend, Apollo, he it was
annotations.note: The god is named twice, without rage. Then comes the 'But.' Read the stanza as one thought: the design was Apollo's, the blow his own.

annotations.quote: Was mine, none other. How,
annotations.note: The enjambed 'How, / How' is Storr straining for rhyme, but the claim is clear. The blinding is the one act he fully owns, and he will defend it as a judgment, not a fit.

annotations.quote: For thou wert better dead than living blind.
annotations.note: Blunt, from friends. It raises the question the whole ending turns on: why did he not follow Jocasta? His answer, in the next speech, is that the dead have eyes too.

links.why: The shepherd's pity, which Oedipus now curses.
The messenger's version of the same act, with a god guiding the steps.
Oedipus answers 'better dead' in full.

s13.essay:
The Chorus have told him he would be better dead, and Oedipus argues back. 'What's done was well done.' I love that he is still arguing. The long speech that follows is a man reasoning out his own punishment, point by point: with what eyes could he have met his father and mother among the dead? How could he look at his children, the city, the statues of the gods? And he remembers who passed sentence: he is cut off 'by my own proclamation.' The curse of [[s3]] has found its man, and he insists on its being carried out. Then the speech stops reasoning and starts calling out to places, Cithaeron, Corinth, the three roads, as if they were witnesses. The crossroads 'drank my blood,' he says, meaning his father's. The confusion of whose blood is whose is the whole story in three words.

Creon's entrance is the last reversal. The man Oedipus wanted dead in [[s5]] now holds every power over him, and Sophocles makes him neither vengeful nor warm. He is correct. He does not gloat; he wants the polluted thing taken indoors out of the sun; he will not grant exile until he has asked the god. There is something chilling in that caution, and something fair: Oedipus acted on quick certainty all day, and here is a ruler who will not. I part company with readers who find Creon noble here. He is decent and small, and the play needs the contrast.

The scene with the daughters is where the play finally lets itself be tender, and it is not sentimental. Oedipus cannot see them; he feels for them with the hands that put his eyes out, and names those hands exactly. What he foresees for them is not tragedy but social shame: festivals they will leave in tears, no husbands. It is a father's small practical worrying, and it hurts more than the grand laments. He asks Creon to be their father and then, told to let them go, cries 'Rob me not of these my children!' Creon's answer is the play's last word on him: 'Crave not mastery in all.' Even now he wants to command.

Notice that the ending withholds what was promised. The oracle demanded the killer's expulsion; Oedipus begs for it; and he is led back into the house. Nothing is resolved except knowledge.

The Chorus close with the moral: count no man happy until he is dead. It is true to [[s10]] and, I think, much smaller than the play we have just read.

annotations.quote: What’s done was well done. Thou canst never shake
annotations.note: The old imperious tone, intact. Blind and ruined, he is still certain, still closing the discussion ('A truce to argument'). The catastrophe has changed what he knows, not who he is.

annotations.quote: By my own proclamation ’gainst the wretch,
annotations.note: He is judge, prosecutor, criminal and now executioner of his own decree. No one else in Thebes has had to lift a hand.

annotations.quote: Ye triple high-roads, and thou hidden glen,
annotations.note: He speaks to the crossroads as to a living witness. Jocasta's passing detail from [[s5]] has become a place he will carry behind his eyes for good.

annotations.quote: Be heard by kin and seen by kin alone.
annotations.note: Creon's instinct is to shut the doors Oedipus has just thrown open. One man wants to be seen for what he is; the other thinks about what is seemly. 'Kin' is a hard word to hear in this family.

annotations.quote: It first behooved me to consult the god.
annotations.note: Creon went to Delphi in the prologue and proposes to go again. It is prudence, and it is also a refusal to take any decision on himself.

annotations.quote: A brother’s hands, a father’s; hands that made
annotations.note: He will not let even an embrace pass without stating the truth of it. The same honesty that drove the inquiry now makes him say to two small girls what he is to them.

annotations.quote: Crave not mastery in all,
annotations.note: The verse shifts into a longer, quicker line for this last exchange, and Creon gets the final say. It is a just rebuke and an ungenerous one, spoken to a blind man holding his daughters.

annotations.quote: Therefore wait to see life’s ending ere thou count one mortal blest;
annotations.note: A proverb the Greeks credited to Solon. It is sound, and it explains very little about a man who was not merely unlucky but who chose, at every turn, to know.

links.why: The proclamation and curse Oedipus now applies to himself, and Teiresias' picture of the blind exile.
Oedipus condemning Creon unheard; the positions are now reversed.
The first sight of the king among suppliant children, against this last one.

characters.name: Oedipus
characters.desc:
The king of Thebes, married to Jocasta, and celebrated for solving the Sphinx's riddle. He bears old injuries to his feet, associated with the meaning of his name, often rendered as swollen-foot. The play provides little other detail about his appearance.

Intelligent, energetic and decisive, he takes the city's suffering personally and wants a clear explanation. His determination can turn into impatience and suspicion when others hesitate. He is accustomed to solving problems and expects inquiry to bring a solution.
characters.why: I read him as a good and formidable man whose virtues, quickness, thoroughness and a refusal to leave a question alone, are the instruments of his ruin. The play is his investigation of himself.

characters.name: Jocasta
characters.role: Queen of Thebes, wife of Oedipus, widow of Laius
characters.desc:
The queen of Thebes, widow of the former king Laius and now wife of Oedipus. She is Creon's sister. The play identifies her through these family and political relationships rather than a detailed physical portrait.

Composed and practical, she tries to settle quarrels and reassure those around her. She is skeptical of claims made for prophecy and draws on remembered experience when arguing. Her attention to the emotional cost of an inquiry can differ from Oedipus' insistence on pursuing it.
characters.why: She is the play's sceptic, and her scepticism is grief. Her long silence in the Third Episode is the moment the truth first lands on anyone.

characters.name: Creon
characters.desc:
Jocasta's brother and a trusted member of the royal household. At the opening he returns from consulting Apollo's oracle at Delphi on the city's behalf. His appearance is not described in detail.

Measured, cautious and concerned with his standing, he answers accusations with orderly reasoning. He distinguishes the advantages of influence from the burdens of kingship. His controlled manner makes a useful contrast to Oedipus' urgency and quick temper.
characters.why: He is the measure of ordinary prudence beside Oedipus: correct, cautious and smaller. The reversal of power between them frames the play.

characters.name: Antigone and Ismene
characters.desc:
Oedipus and Jocasta's young daughters. They have no developed speaking roles in this play and no detailed physical portraits. Their identities matter through the family to which they belong.

Their youth and dependence bring the household's future into view. They are separate from the adult Antigone and Ismene whose arguments drive Antigone, the later story in the Theban sequence. Here, the reader chiefly encounters them through their father's concern for his children.
characters.why: They turn the catastrophe from an idea into a family. His fear for them is the most ordinary and most painful thing he says.

characters.name: Teiresias
characters.desc:
An elderly, blind prophet of Apollo, accompanied by a guide. His blindness is the most important physical feature the play gives him. He is respected for a knowledge that ordinary sight does not provide.

Grave and reluctant to speak, he knows that an answer can bring pain rather than relief. When pressed, he becomes forceful and unyielding. His exchanges with Oedipus connect the play's questions about knowledge with its repeated images of seeing and not seeing.
characters.why: He sets the terms of the play's imagery, the blind man who sees against the sighted man who does not. He also shows that being told the truth is not the same as knowing it.

characters.name: Messenger from Corinth
characters.role: An old shepherd, bringer of news
characters.desc:
An old man who comes from Corinth with news about its royal household. He once worked as a shepherd. The play gives his age and occupation more emphasis than his appearance.

Friendly, talkative and eager to bring reassurance, he does not initially share the concerns of those questioning him. His recollections connect Corinth with the mountain country near Thebes. Listen for the difference between the news he intends to deliver and the information his answers supply.
characters.why: A cheerful man hoping for a tip, and the clearest case of the play's rule that kindness and good news do the damage.

characters.name: Herdsman of Laius
characters.role: An old slave of the royal house
characters.desc:
An elderly servant and shepherd from the household of Laius, the previous king. He has spent years in the hill pastures and is summoned because of what he may remember. His physical portrait is limited chiefly to his age.

Reluctant and fearful under questioning, he resists saying more than he must. Longstanding loyalty, memories and compassion all bear on his testimony. He is distinct from the messenger from Corinth, though their earlier work as shepherds connects their accounts.
characters.why: He holds both halves of the secret, the murder and the birth. His pity for a baby is the hinge of the whole story.

characters.name: Priest of Zeus
characters.desc:
An older priest who speaks for the people gathered as suppliants at the palace. Children and elderly citizens accompany him at the altars, carrying the visible signs of a religious appeal.

Respectful and urgent, he describes the city's plague and asks Oedipus for help. He treats the king as an exceptionally capable human being, rather than a god. His appeal establishes the public trust and responsibility under which Oedipus begins the inquiry.
characters.why: He fixes the height Oedipus falls from, and names in advance the epitaph the play goes on to write.

characters.name: Chorus of Theban Elders
characters.desc:
A group of older male citizens of Thebes who remain present through the main action. They sing between scenes and sometimes speak through a leader. Their shared civic identity is more important than individual appearances.

Loyal to the city and its king, they are anxious about divine authority and hesitant to accept grave accusations. They try to steady heated arguments. Their changing confidence helps the reader follow what the evidence means to people hearing it for the first time.
characters.why: They are the nearest thing to us on stage: they hear everything, believe what decent people would believe, and are wrong until the end. Their odes track the city's trust as it strains and turns to mourning.

characters.name: Second Messenger
characters.desc:
A servant from inside the Theban palace, distinct from the old messenger who arrives from Corinth. He brings an account of events within the royal household; the play does not give him a detailed physical description.

He is an emotionally affected witness who tries to explain what he saw and what lay beyond his sight. His narrative carries private events into the public space of the stage. Keeping the two messengers separate helps clarify the origins and reliability of their news.
characters.why: The violence reaches us only through him, including his admission of what he could not see.

movements.name: The Plague and the Vow
movements.desc: Oedipus swears to find the killer of Laius, curses him, and is told by Teiresias that he is the man, which nobody can believe.

movements.name: The Crossroads
movements.desc: A quarrel with Creon gives way to Jocasta's story of the three roads, and Oedipus begins to fear he killed the king.

movements.name: The Two Shepherds
movements.desc: News from Corinth turns the question from who killed Laius to who Oedipus is, and the herdsman answers it.

movements.name: The Open Doors
movements.desc: Jocasta's death and the blinding are reported, and Oedipus comes out to be seen, to judge himself, and to part from his daughters.
